unit.title: Cut bend and install electrical conduits

summary: This unit is for Level 3 trainees who plan, lead and check conduit work. You will learn to choose the right conduit system for a Jamaican site, work out stubs, offsets, saddles, fill and expansion, and cut, thread and bend steel and PVC conduit without faults. You will also learn to fix and finish runs that keep their earth path and keep out water and fire, and to check, test and record the work of a team.

blocks.p: At Level 2 you learned to cut, bend and fix conduit under supervision. At Level 3 you are expected to **plan the job, work out the bends, lead a small team, check their work and hand over a tested, recorded installation**. This kit goes deeper into why each step is done, so that you can choose the best method for each job and explain it to the people you lead.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read the job information
Use the drawings, the specification and the makers' data to find the conduit type, size, finish, routes, box positions, fill and bending limits and tests.
Plan the work and lead the team
Walk the route, find clashes, do a take-off, place draw-in points, set the order of work, give each person a clear task and brief them on the risks.
Work safely
Isolate any existing circuit you work near, control dust, heat guns, solvent cement and sharp swarf, and choose safe access for work at height.
Choose the conduit system
Pick steel, PVC or flexible conduit, the finish and the fittings that suit the place: sun, salt air, damp, concrete, machines or fire-rated walls.
Do the calculations
Work out stub marks, offsets (multiplier and shrink), saddles, bend lengths, total bending, cable fill, expansion and quantities, and check them.
Cut, ream and thread
Cut square, remove every burr, and cut clean threads of the right length on heavy-gauge steel.
Bend steel and PVC
Make bends, offsets and saddles to the right angle, in line, with no flattening, kinks or twist, using the right bender, spring or heat.
Fix and join the run
Fix runs level and plumb with the right supports and fixings, make tight joints and box entries, allow for expansion, drainage and fire stopping.
Test, inspect and draw in
Test the earth continuity of steel runs, inspect every run against a checklist, swab it and organise the drawing in of cables.
Record and hand over
Mark changes on an as-built drawing, complete test records and a snag list, and leave the site clean and safe.

ul: The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, but many specifications, drawings and fittings use British terms. You will meet both: **EMT** (thin-wall steel tubing) and **RMC/IMC** (US rigid steel conduit) beside British **heavy-gauge screwed conduit**; US **conduit bodies** (such as an LB) beside British **draw-in boxes**; 'conduit fill' beside 'space factor'. This kit gives both.

Conduit sizes come in two systems. US conduit has a trade size in inches (½, ¾, 1 inch) with a metric designator (16, 21, 27). British and European conduit is sized by its outside diameter in millimetres (20, 25, 32 mm). **A ¾-inch conduit is not a 20 mm conduit**: the threads and fittings do not match, so never mix them on one job.

The climate is hard on conduit: strong sun breaks down ordinary PVC and makes it grow and shrink; salt air near the coast rusts steel and fixings; heavy rain, humidity and hurricanes call for sealed boxes, drains and strong fixings.

New and altered installations must be inspected and certified before JPS connects them; this is overseen by the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)**. On many jobs the inspector or the client's engineer will want to see concealed conduit before it is covered, so plan for that.

blocks.note: Follow the specification and the code the job is designed to. Where this kit gives a figure (a multiplier, a fill percentage, a support distance), it is a typical one: the specification, the maker's data and your instructor have the final say.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The sections follow a real job: planning and safety first, then choosing materials, the calculations, cutting and bending, fixing, testing and handover. Work every example with a calculator as you read. Then try the practice test and read every explanation, even when you get the question right.

sections.title: Planning and leading a conduit job

blocks.p: Most conduit faults are planning faults: a route that clashes with a beam, a run with too many bends to pull, boxes at the wrong height, or not enough fittings on site. As the Level 3 person you plan **before anyone cuts conduit**.

head: Document
What you take from it
rows: Drawings (layout and details)
Routes, box and board positions, heights, which circuits share a run, and where the run crosses walls, beams and other services. Check the revision letter: work only from the latest issue.
Specification
Conduit type, size and finish; fittings; support spacing; fill and bending limits; expansion, fire stopping and segregation rules; the tests and records needed.
Makers' data
Bending charts (take-up and radius), inside areas for fill, expansion figures and coupling settings, support spacing, solvent cement times, IP ratings.
Risk assessment and method statement
The hazards of the job and the agreed safe way of working, including isolation and access.
Programme
When each area is ready for you, when slabs are poured and ceilings closed, and when the job must be finished.

ul: Take the drawing round the site and check each route, box position and height. Heights are measured from the **finished floor level**, not the bare slab.
Look for clashes: beams, columns, ducts, water and drain pipes, doors and windows, and the work of other trades.
Note the surface for each fixing (concrete, block, timber, steel) and anything hot, wet or likely to be knocked.
Check access: ladders, podium steps or a mobile tower, and where materials can be stored and bent.
Mark the routes on the wall or ceiling with a chalk line or laser level once they are agreed.

blocks.note: **Never drill, notch, cut or weld a structural beam, column or slab** to get a conduit through, even if the drawing seems to show the route going through it. Stop, report the clash to your supervisor and agree a new route in writing. Only the structural engineer can approve a hole in a structural member.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Item
How to count it
rows: Conduit

Add up the length of every run from the drawing, allow for drops to boxes and for bends, then add a waste allowance (often about 10%). Divide by the length supplied, usually 3 m (10 ft) or 3.75 m depending on the maker, and round up.
Couplings
A straight run of n lengths joined end to end needs n − 1 couplings. Add couplings where you join off-cuts.
Saddles
Run length ÷ spacing gives the number of spaces; add one for the saddles at the ends; then add saddles close to each bend and box.
Boxes and fittings
Count from the drawing: through, angle, tee and terminal boxes, adaptable boxes, draw-in boxes or conduit bodies, expansion couplings, unions, drains.
Bushes, locknuts, glands
One set at every box entry or knockout.
Fixings and consumables
Screws, plugs or anchors to suit each surface; cutting oil, zinc-rich paint, solvent cement and cleaner, fire-stopping product, draw wire.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A straight surface run is 26 m long, in 3 m lengths, with saddles every 1.2 m. Conduit: 26 ÷ 3 = 8.7, so 9 lengths; with 10% for waste, 28.6 m ÷ 3 = 9.5, so order 10 lengths. Couplings: 9 lengths joined end to end need 8. Saddles: 26 ÷ 1.2 = 21.7, so 22 spaces and 23 saddles, plus extra ones beside any bends and boxes.

Every bend adds friction when cables are pulled in. Specifications therefore limit the **total bending between draw-in points** (the NEC limit is 360° between pull points) and the length of a run. Plan draw-in boxes or inspection fittings so that each part of the run stays within the limit, and so that each one can still be reached after the ceiling and finishes are in.

blocks.h: Order of work and team roles

flow: Plan, take-off and order materials
Brief the team on the plan and the risks
Set out routes and box positions
Fix boxes and fixing points
Measure, cut, ream, thread and bend each length
Fix and join the run, check level and plumb
Inspect and test earth continuity
Swab, draw in cables, record and hand over

ul: Give each person a clear task that suits their skill, and pair a less experienced trainee with an experienced one.
Name a **stage leader** for each stage (planning, bending, fixing, testing) who checks the others' work before the next stage starts.
Check the first piece of each person's work closely, then keep checking at stages, not only at the end, while faults are still easy to put right.

blocks.note: Write every calculation on a calculation sheet with the figures you used: depth, angle, multiplier, shrink, take-up. Then a second person can check it before conduit is cut, and you have a record for the assessor and the client.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Conduit work brings together electrical, height, dust, heat, fire and manual-handling hazards. The risk assessment must cover each one, and you, as the person leading, must see that the controls are actually used.

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Existing circuits: extending from a box or board that is in use, or drilling near hidden cables
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Scan with a cable and pipe detector and check the drawings before drilling.
Work at height: long runs along ceilings and high walls

A mobile tower or podium steps, set up and checked by a trained person, wheels locked, guardrails fitted. Never stand a stepladder on a bench or lean a ladder on the conduit run. Keep people from under the work.
Dust from chasing and drilling block and concrete (it contains silica, which damages the lungs)
A wall chaser or drill with dust extraction, dust masks of the right grade, goggles; clean up with a vacuum, never by dry sweeping; keep other people out of the area.
Noise from chasers, hammer drills and chop saws
Ear protection; warn others; work noisy tasks at agreed times in occupied buildings.
Sharp ends, burrs and swarf
Ream and file every end; wear gloves; clear swarf with a brush, never with bare hands.
Heat guns and solvent cement for PVC
Solvent cement and cleaner give off flammable vapour: keep lids on, work with good airflow, and keep heat guns, grinders and sparks well away. Never leave a heat gun switched on and unattended.
Threading and cutting oil
Secure the conduit in a pipe vice; keep hands clear of the die; wipe up oil spills at once so nobody slips.
Carrying 3 m lengths
Carry them low and level with a partner for bundles; look out for people, light fittings and overhead lines when turning.
Heat in roof spaces and on roofs
Work early in the day, take short spells with water breaks, and watch each other for heat exhaustion.

flow: Identify the circuit from the panel schedule
Tell the occupants the supply is going off
Switch off and lock off with your own padlock
Fit a danger tag
Prove the tester on a proving unit
Test at the box between all conductors
Prove the tester again
Only then open the box and work

blocks.note: If the tester gives no reading at the box and then also gives no reading on the proving unit afterwards, the test proves nothing. Treat the circuit as live, get a working tester and repeat the whole test.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Brief the team before work starts: the hazards, the controls, the access equipment, where the first-aid kit is and who to tell if something goes wrong.
Check PPE and tools at the start of each day: safety glasses, gloves, dust masks, ear protection, sound leads and tools inside their test dates.
Stop work that is unsafe at once, explain why, and show the safe way. A trainee copies what the leader does, not what the leader says.

blocks.p: The specification usually names the conduit system, but at Level 3 you must understand why, spot a choice that will not survive the site, and query it in writing before work starts.

head: Conduit
What it is
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Heavy-gauge screwed steel (British); rigid metal conduit (RMC) and intermediate metal conduit (IMC) (US)
Thick-walled steel tube, joined with threaded couplings and fittings
Strong protection: plant rooms, workshops, low level where knocks are likely, exposed outdoor runs where steel is specified
Heavy and slow to install; threads must be protected; rusts if the finish is damaged
Light-gauge steel; electrical metallic tubing (EMT)
Thin-walled steel tube, not threaded; joined with set-screw or compression couplings
Indoor surface and ceiling runs in dry places; quick to bend with a hand bender
Less strength; set-screw fittings are for dry places only, compression fittings for damp places
Rigid PVC (light, medium and heavy grades; US Schedule 40 and 80)
Plastic tube joined with solvent cement
Corrosive and coastal sites, damp places, cast into concrete (heavy grade), and outdoors when UV-resistant
Large expansion with heat; ordinary grades break down in sun; softens near hot surfaces; needs a separate earth conductor
Flexible metal conduit and liquid-tight flexible conduit
Spiral steel strip, with a plastic jacket on the liquid-tight type
The last short length to motors, pumps and machines that vibrate or move
Not a reliable earth path on its own: run a separate protective conductor
Flexible PVC (corrugated) conduit
Light plastic tube that bends by hand
Some concealed runs in walls and slabs, where the specification allows it
Easily crushed; not for exposed runs

head: Finish
Where it suits
Notes
rows: Black enamel
Dry indoor places only
Rusts quickly wherever it is scratched, cut or threaded.
**Hot-dip galvanised** (dipped in molten zinc)
Outdoors, damp and humid places, plant rooms
The zinc protects the steel even where it is slightly scratched. Paint cut threads and damage with zinc-rich paint after assembly.
Stainless steel, or PVC-coated steel
Very corrosive places: right by the sea, chemical stores, some food plants
Costly; use only matching fittings.

blocks.note: Keep **one finish and one metal** throughout a system: galvanised conduit with galvanised boxes and fittings, stainless with stainless. Where different metals or finishes touch in damp, salty air, one corrodes the other at the joint, and the joint is also the earth path.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Situation
Best choice
Why
rows: Open roof or wall near the sea, in full sun
UV-resistant PVC with stainless or plastic fixings and expansion couplings
No rust in salt air; UV grade resists the sun; couplings take the large expansion.
Cast into a concrete slab or column
Heavy-gauge conduit made for concrete, with sealed joints and capped ends
It must survive the pour and vibration without crushing or letting in grout.
Plant room, workshop or low level where trolleys and machines can strike it
Heavy-gauge galvanised steel
Resists knocks; can be part of the earth path where allowed.
Motor on a slide base, pump or compressor
Rigid conduit to a box, then a short flexible or liquid-tight flexible length, with a separate protective conductor
Takes vibration and movement without cracking or loosening.
Hotel or food-plant kitchen, laundry
Galvanised steel or PVC with sealed, IP-rated boxes, spaced off the wall where cleaning matters
Steam, grease and washing; no ledges for dirt and pests.
Hollow walls and ceilings in offices
Concealed PVC or EMT fixed before the finishes, with draw-in points left reachable
Hidden, but cables can still be replaced later.

head: Fitting
Use
rows: Through, angle, tee and terminal boxes (circular boxes)
Change direction or end a run, and hold a light or accessory; the conduit screws into threaded spouts.
Adaptable boxes
Square boxes with knockouts, for junctions and where several runs meet.
Draw-in boxes, inspection bends and tees; US conduit bodies (LB, LL, LR, T, C)
Fittings with removable lids, placed so cables can be pulled in in stages and reached later.
Couplings
Join two lengths in a straight line.
Unions and split couplings
Join two fixed lengths when neither can be turned.
Male bushes, locknuts and insulating bushings
Clamp the conduit to a box at a knockout, make the earth path and give the cables a smooth edge.
Expansion couplings
A sliding joint that lets a PVC run grow and shrink.
Drain and breather fittings
Let condensed water out at the low points of outdoor and damp runs.
Saddles: standard, spacer-bar (distance) and sliding
Fix the run to the surface; spacer-bar saddles hold it clear of the wall; sliding saddles let PVC move.

blocks.p: An **IP code** (ingress protection), such as IP65, shows how well a box or fitting keeps out solids and water. The first digit is for solids, the second for water. A higher number gives more protection.

head: Digit
First digit: solids
Second digit: water
rows: Objects over 1 mm, such as wires
Splashing from any direction
Dust-protected: some dust may enter but not enough to harm
Low-pressure water jets
Dust-tight
Powerful water jets, such as a wash-down hose
Short immersion (up to 1 m)
Continuous immersion, as the maker states

blocks.note: Equipment made to US standards shows a **NEMA type** instead: for example 3R (rainproof, outdoors), 4 (watertight, for hose-down) and 4X (watertight and corrosion-resistant, good for coastal and wash-down sites).
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Bending is quick and accurate only when the marks are right. These calculations tell you where to put the marks. Always use the bender maker's chart for your size of conduit, and try an unfamiliar bend on an off-cut first.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Stub (stub-up)
A 90° bend that turns the conduit up a wall or into a box.
Take-up (deduct)
The amount the bender 'takes up' in a 90° bend. You subtract it from the stub height to find the mark. It comes from the maker's chart.
Offset
Two equal bends in opposite directions that move the run sideways, out from a wall or round an obstacle.
Depth (rise)
How far the offset or saddle moves the conduit sideways.
Multiplier
The number you multiply the depth by to get the distance between the two bend marks of an offset.
Shrink
The length an offset or saddle uses up, so that the conduit ends up shorter along the wall than it was.
Saddle
A set of bends that lifts the run over an obstacle and brings it back to the same line: three bends or four.
Kick
A single bend of less than 90°, used to move a run away from the surface.

blocks.p: Measure the stub height you need, from the end of the conduit to the back of the finished bend. **Mark = stub height − take-up.** Put the bender's mark (on many US hand benders, the arrow) on your mark and bend to 90°.
**Worked example.** The chart gives a take-up of 125 mm for this size. You need a stub 450 mm high. Mark = 450 − 125 = **325 mm** from the end of the conduit.
**Distance between the bend marks = depth × multiplier. Shrink = depth × shrink factor.** The multiplier is 1 ÷ the sine of the bend angle, which is why it gets bigger as the angle gets smaller.
**Worked example.** A run must step out 120 mm to pass a pilaster, using two 45° bends. Distance between marks = 120 × 1.4 = **168 mm** (use 170 mm). Shrink = 120 × 0.41 = **about 50 mm**.

flow: Measure from a fixed point (a box or the board) to where the offset must be finished
Add the shrink to that measurement
Mark the bend nearest the obstacle, then the other bend one 'multiplier distance' away, on the same side of the conduit
Make the first bend to the angle
Turn the conduit exactly half a turn
Line up the second mark and make the second bend
Check the depth, and that both legs are parallel and not twisted

blocks.note: If you take the shrink off instead of adding it, the offset finishes short by twice the shrink. If you forget to turn the conduit half a turn between the bends, the two bends go the same way and you get a single bend of twice the angle, not an offset.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Angle
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Shallow: 10°, 22½°, 30°
Less bending added to the run, so cables pull in more easily; less shrink; neat on shallow steps
The offset is long, so it needs more straight wall; the marks must be measured carefully
Short offset, fits tight spaces
More bending added (two 45° bends add 90°; two 60° bends add 120°), more shrink and a harder pull

blocks.p: So on a run that already has several bends, a deep offset made with two 22½° bends (45° in all) is often better than one made with two 45° bends (90° in all), if there is room for it.
A **three-bend saddle** lifts the run over a small obstacle, such as a pipe, and brings it back to the same line. The usual set is a **45° bend in the middle and 22½° bends each side**. For this set:

ul: Put the centre mark over the centre of the obstacle. The saddle uses up about **0.19 (3/16) of its depth** in length in all, so when you measure from a fixed point, add **half of that** (about 0.1 × the depth) to the distance to the centre mark.
Put each outer mark about **2½ times the saddle depth** from the centre mark.
Bend the centre 45° first, then the two 22½° bends the other way, each in line with the first.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A run must cross a 40 mm pipe. Saddle depth 40 mm. Outer marks 2.5 × 40 = **100 mm** each side of the centre mark. Total shrink is about 0.19 × 40 = 8 mm, so add half of it, **about 4 mm**, to the measured distance to the centre mark.

A **four-bend saddle** is two offsets back to back: one up, a straight section across the obstacle, then one down. Use it for wide obstacles such as a beam or a run of pipes. Work out each offset as above.

blocks.note: On many US hand benders the head is marked to help: an **arrow** for the stub mark, a **star** for the back of a 90° bend, and a notch or teardrop for the centre of a three-bend saddle. Learn the marks on the bender you are using.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Calculations: bend lengths, bending limits, fill and expansion

blocks.p: The curved part of a bend is part of a circle. **Length = 2 × π × centre-line radius × (angle ÷ 360).** For a 90° bend this is π × r ÷ 2, about **1.57 × r**.

**Worked example.** A 90° bend with a centre-line radius of 120 mm uses 1.57 × 120 = **about 188 mm** of conduit. A 45° bend of the same radius uses half of that: about 94 mm. You need this when you cut a length to fit exactly between two fixed points.
Add every bend between two draw-in points, including both bends of each offset and all three or four bends of a saddle.

**Worked example.** A run has two 90° bends, one offset of two 45° bends and one three-bend saddle (45° and two 22½°). Total = 90 + 90 + 45 + 45 + 45 + 22½ + 22½ = **360°**. That is right at the NEC limit. If the route needs one more bend, add a draw-in point.

Cables must not fill more than a set part of the conduit's inside area. This part, given as a percentage, is the **space factor** (US: conduit fill). Too many cables are hard to pull in, so the insulation gets scraped and stretched, and packed cables cannot lose their heat in use.

head: Number of cables (NEC)
Largest fill of the inside area
rows: 1 cable
2 cables
3 or more cables

blocks.p: British-style specifications use cable factors and conduit factors from tables, which work in the same way and also allow for the length of the run and the number of bends. Use the method the specification names.

flow: Find the conduit's inside area from the maker's data
Find each cable's area over its insulation (π × diameter² ÷ 4, or from the cable data)
Allowed area = inside area × fill percentage
Add up the cable areas
If the cables add up to more than the allowed area, use a bigger conduit or split the circuits

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A conduit has an inside area of 250 mm² and the specification allows 40%. Allowed area = 0.4 × 250 = 100 mm². Each cable takes 9.6 mm². 100 ÷ 9.6 = 10.4, so **10 cables** at most. Always round down.

PVC grows much more with heat than steel: roughly **0.05 to 0.08 mm per metre for each 1 °C**, depending on the maker (exam questions often use 0.06). Steel grows only about 0.012 mm per metre per °C. In Jamaica a conduit on a sunny wall or roof can be 30 to 40 °C hotter in the afternoon than at night.
**Change in length = expansion figure × length in metres × temperature change in °C.**
**Worked example.** An 18 m run on a sunny wall warms from 25 °C to 60 °C, a change of 35 °C. Change = 0.06 × 18 × 35 = **about 38 mm**.

If the run is fixed hard at both ends, that growth makes it bow out between saddles, pull out of boxes or crack joints, and when it cools it pulls joints apart. The NEC asks for **expansion fittings on rigid PVC where the expected change in a straight run between fixed points is 6 mm or more**. That covers almost every outdoor run in Jamaica.
The coupling has a sliding barrel with a fixed amount of travel. Set it for the temperature on the day so that it has room both to close (as the run grows) and to open (as it shrinks).

head: Conduit temperature when you fix it
Set the coupling
Because
rows: Near the coolest it will be (early morning, shade)
Mostly open
The run will mostly grow from here, closing the coupling.
About half-way through its range
About half open
It will grow and shrink by about the same amount.
Near the hottest it will be (afternoon sun)
Mostly closed
The run will mostly shrink from here, opening the coupling.

blocks.p: To be exact: **room to close = expansion figure × length × (highest temperature − temperature now)**. The maker's instructions usually include a setting chart. Fix the run hard only where the maker says (often next to one end of each coupling), and use saddles that let it slide everywhere else.

Work out how many pieces you can cut from each length before you cut. **Worked example.** Pieces 700 mm long from a 3 m length: 3000 ÷ 700 = 4.3, so **4 pieces**, with 200 mm left over (less the saw cuts). Use the off-cuts for short drops, not for joints in the middle of a long run.

ul: Measure from fixed points (the face of a box, the board, a finished wall), never from the last piece you fixed, so errors do not add up along the run.
Allow for the depth the conduit goes into a box spout or coupling.
Mark all round the conduit with a fine marker or a wrap-round guide so the cut is square.

head: Tool
Use
Notes
rows: Hacksaw
Steel and PVC conduit
Use a fine blade: about 24 teeth per 25 mm for heavy-gauge steel and 32 for thin-wall. Hold the conduit in a pipe vice; cut square with steady full strokes.
Wheel pipe cutter
Heavy-gauge steel
Cuts square and fast, but the wheel rolls a **larger burr into the bore**, so the end needs more reaming.
PVC cutter or fine-tooth saw
PVC conduit
Clean, square cuts; deburr inside and out.
Abrasive chop saw
Large amounts of steel
Throws sparks and leaves a heavy, hot burr; use guards, glasses and ear protection, and keep sparks away from PVC cement and flammables.

blocks.p: Every cut end must be **reamed inside** (with a reamer or half-round file) until it is smooth, and filed outside. A burr left inside acts like a knife: it strips the insulation as the cables are pulled past it, and the damage may not show until a fault occurs years later.

flow: Hold the conduit in a pipe vice
Ream the end first and file a slight chamfer outside
Fit the right die, the right way round, in the die stock
Start the die square on the conduit
Turn steadily, using plenty of cutting oil
Back off a quarter turn every turn or two to break the swarf
Stop at the right length
Clean off oil and swarf and try a coupling on the thread

ul: **Thread length:** long enough for the two conduit ends to **butt together** in the middle of a coupling, or to screw fully into a box spout, with no more than one or two threads showing. On US tapered threads, a common guide is to stop when the conduit end is level with the far face of the die.
A thread that is too short leaves a gap in the coupling, so the earth path rests on a few threads. A thread that is too long leaves bare thread showing, which rusts.
After assembly, paint any bare thread and damaged zinc with **zinc-rich paint**. Never paint threads before you screw them together: paint inside the joint can break the earth path.
British metric conduit uses parallel threads; US rigid conduit uses tapered pipe threads. They do not mix.

head: Threading fault
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Torn, rough thread
Blunt or chipped die, or no cutting oil
Sharpen or replace the die; use plenty of oil; recut on a fresh end
'Drunken' thread that wobbles
Die not started square
Start square with the die guide; recut
Thread will not start in a coupling
Die fitted the wrong way round, or burr on the end
Fit the die correctly; chamfer the end
Swarf jams the die
Die not backed off often enough
Back off every turn or two; clear the swarf

ul: Use a **hand bender** for small sizes and a few bends. For heavy-gauge 25 mm and larger, or many bends, use a **bending machine** with the **former and guide that match the size** of the conduit; the wrong former flattens the conduit.
Keep the welded **seam on the inside of the bend or at the side**, never on the outside, where the steel stretches and the seam can split.
Steel springs back a little after bending: bend slightly past the angle, then check.
Check every angle with a protractor, angle finder or square, and check that a second bend is **in the same plane** as the first by laying the conduit on the floor: it should lie flat without rocking.

**Cold bending with a spring** suits light and medium grades in the smaller sizes (typically 20 and 25 mm). Use the spring made for that size and grade, tie a cord to it, bend a little past the angle and ease back, then twist the spring anti-clockwise to free it. Do not bend too tight a radius.

**Heat bending** with a heat gun or heating box suits larger sizes, heavy grades and sets the spring cannot make. Warm a length evenly by turning it, with the spring or the maker's insert inside to stop it collapsing, bend it, and **hold it in shape until it has cooled**; otherwise it springs back.
Do not overheat: brown or blistered PVC is weakened and must be cut out.
Factory-made bends and elbows are often the neatest choice for large sizes.

head: Bending fault
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Flattened bend (oval section)
Wrong former or guide; no spring in PVC; bend too tight
Cut it out and remake with the right former, spring or heat
Kinks or wrinkles on the inside
Bent too fast or too tight; PVC too cold or too hot
Remake, bending steadily to a larger radius
Length rocks and will not lie flat (dog-leg)
Second bend twisted out of line with the first
Remake, keeping both bends in one plane
Offset depth wrong
Wrong multiplier, or marks measured from different sides
Recalculate; mark both bends on the same side
Single double-angle bend instead of an offset
Conduit not turned half a turn before the second bend
Remake, turning exactly 180°
PVC bend springs back
Released before it cooled
Reheat gently and hold until cool

blocks.note: A flattened or kinked bend must be **remade**, not hidden with an extra saddle or paint. It reduces the bore, damages cables as they are pulled through and fails the inspection.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Fixing, joining and finishing the run

blocks.p: Take the spacing of supports from the **specification or the maker's tables**, because it depends on the type of conduit, its size, whether it runs horizontally or vertically, and the temperature. PVC needs closer supports than steel, horizontal runs closer than vertical ones, and hot places closer still.

ul: Fit a saddle close to **each box, each side of each bend and each coupling** (often within about 300 mm). Even spacing that misses the bends lets them sag and strains the joints.

NEC examples: **EMT** must be supported within 900 mm of each box and at least every 3 m; **rigid PVC** within 900 mm of each box, with closer spacing along the run for small sizes (900 mm for the ½ to 1 inch sizes). Always check the edition and the specification used on your job.

Use the saddle the job needs: standard saddles for most runs, **spacer-bar (distance) saddles** to hold the conduit clear of the wall in kitchens, food plants and damp places, and **sliding saddles** on PVC runs with expansion couplings.
Exposed runs in hurricane-prone places may need closer or stronger fixings; follow the specification.

head: Surface
Fixing
rows: Concrete and solid block
Wall plugs and screws of the right size, or anchors for heavy loads; drill to the plug's depth and clear the dust from the hole.
Hollow block
Plugs or anchors made for hollow material; avoid fixing into the hollow cores where the maker says so.
Timber (trusses, joists)
Wood screws of the right gauge and length straight into the timber; never masonry nails, plugs or cable ties.
Steel beams and purlins
Beam clamps or strut channel; never weld or drill structural steel without approval.
Near the sea
Stainless-steel or suitable plastic fixings; plated steel rusts within months.

blocks.p: Check long runs with a **laser level or a long spirit level at many points**, not by eye or from one end. Set out the line first with a chalk line or laser, fix the saddles to it, then fix the conduit. Vertical drops are checked with a level or plumb line.

ul: **Steel:** screw each length fully into couplings and box spouts so that the ends butt and the joint is tight on clean metal. At knockouts use a coupling outside and a **male bush inside**, or locknuts and an insulating bushing, tightened so the box wall is clamped.
Where two fixed lengths must be joined and neither can turn, use a **union or split coupling**, not a coupling forced onto a bent length.
**EMT:** tighten set screws or compression nuts fully; use compression fittings in damp places.

**PVC:** cut square and deburr, clean both parts, apply the right solvent cement to both, push fully home with a slight twist and hold for the time the maker gives. Cement works faster in Jamaican heat, so cement one joint at a time and keep the tin closed.
Outdoor and damp runs collect water from rain and from **condensation**: warm, humid air inside the conduit cools and leaves water behind.
Avoid low points (water traps) in the run. Where one cannot be avoided, fit a **drain fitting** at the lowest point.
Bring conduits into outdoor boxes from the side or from below where possible, and seal entries with the right gland or adaptor.
Where a conduit passes from a cold, air-conditioned area into a hot, humid one, **seal it at the boundary** with a suitable compound so damp air cannot move through it and condense.
Close every unused knockout and fit lids and gaskets so the box keeps its IP rating.

blocks.h: Fire stopping and keeping services apart

ul: Where a conduit passes through a **fire-rated wall or floor**, seal the gap round it with an **approved fire-stopping product**, installed exactly as its tested detail says (gap size, depth, both faces). If the hole is larger than the product allows, make it good first. Photograph and record each one before it is hidden.
Never use paper, draught-proofing foam or ordinary filler: they do not hold back fire.
Keep power conduits apart from **data and communication** cables, as the specification says, using separate conduits.
Keep conduits clear of hot pipes, flues and steam lines: heat lowers the current a cable can carry and ages its insulation.
In slabs and columns, tie the conduit and boxes firmly to the steel, seal every joint, and **cap or plug every open end** so grout and concrete cannot get in.
Agree the positions and the date of the pour with the builder, and have the work checked before the concrete is placed.
In block walls, cut chases with a chaser and extraction, no deeper than the specification allows, and never chase horizontally across a wall without approval.

blocks.p: Where equipment vibrates or moves (a motor on a slide base, a pump, a compressor), run the rigid conduit to a fixed box near it and finish with a **short length of flexible or liquid-tight flexible conduit** and the right glands. Leave a little slack so the motor can be adjusted, and run a **separate protective conductor**: flexible conduit is not a reliable earth path.

sections.title: Earth continuity, inspection, drawing in and records

blocks.h: Steel conduit as an earth path

blocks.p: Where the code and the specification allow it, steel conduit, boxes and fittings can carry earth fault current back to the board, so that the protective device trips. Then **every joint is part of the earth path** and must conduct well.

head: What breaks the earth path
Prevention
rows: Loose couplings, locknuts or set screws
Tighten every joint; check them at inspection
Paint or rust on threads and box entries
Never paint threads before assembly; keep finishes matched; protect bare thread after assembly
A knockout entry with no bush or locknut inside
Fit a male bush or locknut and bushing so the box wall is clamped
A cracked weld seam or a damaged length
Inspect lengths; cut out damaged sections
A PVC length or fitting put into a steel run
Keep systems separate; bond across any non-metal part with a protective conductor
Flexible conduit
Always run a separate protective conductor

blocks.note: Many Jamaican specifications ask for a **separate green (or green-and-yellow) protective conductor** in every conduit, even in steel. Then the earth path does not rely on every joint staying tight for 30 years. The conduit itself is still bonded.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Make sure the run is complete and no supply is connected anywhere on it
Use a low-resistance ohmmeter (continuity tester)
Null (zero) the leads, or note their resistance and take it off each reading
Measure from the earth terminal at the board to each box on the run
Compare the readings for runs of similar length
Find and fix any high or unsteady reading
Record each reading with the date and your name

blocks.p: Readings on similar runs should be low and similar. A reading much higher than the others, or one that jumps about when the conduit is moved, points to a loose coupling, locknut or connector, or paint or rust in a joint. Fix it and test again.

ul: The run is complete between outlets: the NEC requires a raceway to be complete before cables are drawn in.
Every end is reamed, every box entry has its bush or bushing, and no sharp edge can touch the cables.
Pull a **brush or swab** through each run to clear water, grit and swarf.
Draw-in points can be reached; lids are available.
Fill is within the limit for the cables to be drawn in.

flow: Check cable sizes and colours against the schedule
Set the drums on a stand at the feed end so they turn freely
Push a fish tape or draw wire through to the next draw-in point
Tape the cables to it in a neat, tapered bundle
One person feeds the cables in straight and parallel while another pulls steadily
Use cable lubricant on long or bent runs
Stop at once if the pull gets hard; find the cause
Leave enough cable at each box and label the ends

blocks.p: The person at the feed end matters as much as the puller: they keep the cables straight, stop them twisting and crossing, and watch for damage as they enter.

head: Stage
Look for
rows: Cutting
Square cuts; every end reamed smooth inside; no burr
Threading
Right length; clean, untorn thread; ends butting in couplings; bare thread protected after assembly
Bending
Right angle and depth; no flattening, kinks or wrinkles; no twist between bends; seam position
Fixing
Saddles at the right spacing and close to boxes and bends; level and plumb; right fixings for the surface
Joints and boxes
Tight couplings; bushes and locknuts fitted; lids, gaskets and blanking plugs in place
Finishing
Expansion couplings set; drains fitted; fire stopping done and recorded; segregation kept

blocks.p: When you find a fault, show the trainee what is wrong and why it matters, have it put right or remade, and check it again. Note faults that keep coming back so that more training can be planned.

head: Record
What it holds
rows: As-built drawing
The routes as actually installed, with every change marked, such as a run moved to clear a pipe
Test record
Continuity readings for each run, with the date, the instrument and the tester's name
Snag list
Every item still to finish or fix, who will do it and by when
Fire-stopping record
Where each seal is, the product used and a photo
Completion report
What was done, changes, test results, open snags, materials used and returned

ul: At the end of each day: clear off-cuts and swarf, store tools, close tins of cement, and cap open conduit ends so dirt and water stay out.
At the end of the job: walk every run with the drawing, then hand the records to your supervisor.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can read drawings, specifications and makers' data to find what a conduit job needs.
I can walk a route, find clashes and report a clash with the structure instead of cutting it.
I can do a take-off of conduit, couplings, saddles, boxes and fixings with a waste allowance.
I can plan draw-in points so that no part of a run has too much bending.
I can lead a team: give clear tasks, brief on risks and check work at stages.
I can name the hazards of conduit work and the control for each one.
I can choose a conduit type, finish and fittings for a coastal, sunny, damp, concrete or machine location, and explain why.
I can explain IP codes and NEMA types well enough to choose a box.
I can work out a stub mark from the take-up.
I can work out an offset with the multiplier and the shrink, and say when a shallow angle is better.
I can mark and make a three-bend saddle.
I can work out the length of a bend, the total bending of a run and the cable fill.
I can work out PVC expansion and set an expansion coupling for the temperature on the day.
I can cut, ream and thread heavy-gauge conduit, and find the cause of a bad thread.
I can bend steel and PVC without flattening, kinking or twist, and say how to cure each fault.
I can fix runs level and plumb with the right supports and fixings for the surface.
I can deal with condensation, fire stopping, segregation and flexible connections correctly.
I can test the earth continuity of a steel run and explain a high reading.
I can organise the drawing in of cables safely.
I can complete an as-built drawing, test record, snag list and completion report.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Mark = stub height − take-up
Stub bends
Offset multipliers for 22½° / 30° / 45° / 60° bends
Shrink per mm of depth for the same angles
45° centre, 22½° each side; outer marks 2½ × depth
Three-bend saddle
1.57 × radius
Length of a 90° bend
NEC limit on bending between pull points
NEC fill for 1 / 2 / 3 or more cables
About 0.06 mm per m per °C
A typical figure for PVC expansion (steel about 0.012)
6 mm
NEC: expected change in a PVC run at which expansion fittings are needed
Couplings for n lengths in a straight run

terms: Conduit body
A US fitting with a removable cover (such as an LB) used to change direction and pull cables; similar to a British inspection fitting.
Distance saddle
A spacer-bar saddle that holds conduit clear of the wall.
Draw-in box
A box with a removable lid, placed along a run so cables can be pulled in stages.
Drain fitting
A fitting at the low point of a run that lets condensed water out.
EMT
Electrical metallic tubing: thin-walled steel conduit joined without threads.
Expansion coupling
A sliding joint that lets a PVC run grow and shrink with temperature.
Fire stopping
Sealing the gap round a conduit where it passes through a fire-rated wall or floor, with an approved product.
Galvanising
A zinc coating put on steel by dipping it in molten zinc (hot-dip galvanising).
IP code
Ingress protection: two digits showing protection against solids and water.
Male bush
A short threaded fitting screwed into a coupling from inside a box, clamping the box wall and protecting cables.
Multiplier
The number that the depth of an offset is multiplied by to find the distance between its bend marks.
Offset
Two equal bends in opposite directions that move a run sideways.
Reaming
Removing the burr from inside a cut conduit end.
Saddle (bend)
Three or four bends that take a run over an obstacle and back to its line.
Shrink
The length an offset or saddle uses up along the run.
Space factor (conduit fill)
The part of a conduit's inside area that cables may fill, as a percentage.
Stub (stub-up)
A 90° bend that turns a run up a wall or into a box.
Take-up
The amount subtracted from a stub height to find the bend mark, from the bender maker's chart.
Union (split coupling)
A fitting that joins two fixed lengths when neither can be turned.

c1.title: Heavy-gauge steel in a Port Antonio bakery
c1.text: Kemar Bryan, a Level 3 trainee, leads two Level 2 trainees, Ricardo and Shanelle, installing 20 mm heavy-gauge galvanised steel conduit in the production room of a bakery in Port Antonio, Portland. Along one wall the run must step out 80 mm to pass the flange of a steel column, and Kemar decides to use two 30° bends. Further along, a 50 mm water pipe is fixed flat to the same wall, and the run must cross it with a three-bend saddle (45° in the middle, 22½° each side). The bakery's food-safety officer has asked for no ledges where flour dust and insects can collect.

c2.title: PVC on a fish market wall in Whitehouse
c2.text: Sanya Gordon, a Level 3 trainee, is planning a surface run of UV-resistant PVC conduit along the sea-facing wall of a new fish market in Whitehouse, Westmoreland. The straight run is 32 m long between two weatherproof boxes. The site engineer expects the conduit to range from about 22 °C on a cool night to about 62 °C in the afternoon sun; take PVC growth as 0.06 mm per metre for each 1 °C. The specification asks for one expansion coupling with 100 mm of travel, stainless-steel fixings, and boxes that will survive the nightly wash-down of the market with a powerful hose.

c3.title: Planning runs for a teaching workshop in Junction
c3.text: Dwight Morrison, a Level 3 trainee, is planning 25 mm steel conduit runs for a new teaching workshop at a skills centre in Junction, St Elizabeth. His first route, from the board to a draw-in box, has four 90° bends and one offset made with two 30° bends. The specification allows no more than 360° of bending between draw-in points, and a cable fill of no more than 40% of the conduit's inside area. The maker's data gives the conduit an inside area of 390 mm², and each cable, measured over its insulation, takes up 14 mm².

c4.title: Checking trainees' work in a Highgate warehouse
c4.text: Tamara Lewis, a Level 3 trainee, is checking the work of two Level 2 trainees on a galvanised steel conduit job in a produce warehouse in Highgate, St Mary. She finds that one 30° offset has come out as a single 60° change of direction; that at a knockout entry to an adaptable box a trainee has fitted a coupling on the outside of the box and nothing on the inside; and that on one run the saddles are spaced evenly at 1.5 m, with none near the two bends, which sag. Before the continuity test she touches the leads of the low-resistance ohmmeter together, and it reads 0.3 Ω.

c5.title: Finishing a hotel laundry in Montego Bay
c5.text: Odane Clarke, a Level 3 trainee, is finishing a steel conduit installation in the laundry of a hotel in Montego Bay, St James, with his supervisor Ms Paulette Henry. The laundry is hot and humid all day. One run passes through a block wall that the drawings mark as fire-rated, into the linen store. The fire-stopping sealant on site is approved for gaps of up to 15 mm round steel conduit, but the hole the builder left leaves a gap of about 40 mm round the conduit. A new steam pipe has been fitted 50 mm from one of the conduit runs.

questions.q: How far apart should the two bend marks be for Kemar's 80 mm offset?
o: 112 mm
208 mm
160 mm
80 mm
questions.why: For 30° bends the multiplier is 2, so 80 × 2 = 160 mm. 112 mm comes from the 45° multiplier (1.4) and 208 mm from the 22½° one (2.6): always use the multiplier for the angle you will actually bend.

questions.q: The offset must be finished 1,500 mm from the board. How should Kemar allow for shrink when he marks the conduit?
o: Add about 22 mm to the 1,500 mm before marking
Take about 22 mm off the 1,500 mm before marking
Add 160 mm, the distance between the two marks
Nothing, since shrink only matters for 45° bends
questions.why: Shrink is the length an offset uses up: about 0.27 × 80 = 22 mm for 30° bends. Adding it to the measurement from the fixed point puts the finished offset where it is needed; taking it off would leave the offset about 44 mm short.

questions.q: For the saddle over the 50 mm pipe, about how far from the centre mark should Shanelle put each outer mark?
o: About 50 mm
About 100 mm
About 250 mm
About 125 mm
questions.why: For a three-bend saddle with a 45° centre bend, the usual rule puts each outer mark 2½ times the saddle depth from the centre: 2.5 × 50 = 125 mm. The centre mark itself goes over the centre of the pipe, with half the saddle's shrink (about 0.1 of the depth) added to the measured distance.

questions.q: Which way of fixing the conduit best meets the food-safety officer's request?
o: Standard saddles that pull the conduit tight to the wall
Distance saddles that hold the conduit clear of the wall
Cable ties round the conduit and the nearby water pipe
Self-adhesive clips stuck onto the painted block wall
questions.why: Distance (spacer-bar) saddles leave a gap behind the conduit, so the wall can be cleaned and dust and insects have nowhere to settle. Tying conduit to a pipe is never acceptable, and adhesive clips will not hold steel conduit.

questions.q: Over the expected temperature range, how much will the 32 m run change in length?
o: About 8 mm, so the coupling is not really needed here
About 77 mm, so the one coupling specified is enough
About 119 mm, so a second expansion coupling is needed
About 38 mm, so sliding saddles alone will take it
questions.why: Change = 0.06 × 32 × (62 − 22) = 0.06 × 32 × 40 = 76.8 mm. Use the temperature range, not the top temperature, which gives the wrong 119 mm. The NEC asks for expansion fittings on PVC where the change is 6 mm or more, so this run clearly needs one.

questions.q: Sanya's team fixes the run at 2 p.m., when the conduit is at about 58 °C. How should the expansion coupling be set?
o: Nearly open, since the run will mostly grow from now on
Exactly half open, whatever the temperature on the day
Fully closed, then cement both ends so it cannot slide
Nearly closed, since the run will mostly shrink from now
questions.why: At 58 °C the conduit is near its longest, so it has little left to grow but a lot to shrink as it cools: about 0.06 × 32 × 36 = 69 mm down to 22 °C. Set the coupling nearly closed, using the maker's setting chart.

questions.q: Which rating should the weatherproof boxes have for the nightly wash-down?
o: IP44
IP55
IP66
IP20
questions.why: The second digit is the water protection: 4 is splashing, 5 is low-pressure jets and 6 is powerful jets, such as a wash-down hose. The first digit 6 means dust-tight. Equipment made to US standards may show NEMA 4X, meaning hose-down and corrosion-resistant.

questions.q: Why does the specification call for stainless-steel screws in the saddles, rather than zinc-plated ones?
o: Stainless screws grip far better in plastic wall plugs
Salt air soon rusts plated screws, and the run loosens
Stainless steel stops the PVC from growing in the sun
Plated screws could make the PVC conduit live in a fault
questions.why: Next to the sea, salt spray attacks thin zinc plating within months. The screws rust, stain the wall and fail, and the run sags or blows loose in a storm. Stainless steel, or a suitable plastic fixing, lasts.

questions.q: How much bending does Dwight's first route have between the board and the draw-in box?
questions.why: Every bend counts, including both bends of the offset: 4 × 90° + 2 × 30° = 420°. That is over the 360° limit, so Dwight must split the route with another draw-in point or change it before any conduit is cut.

questions.q: What is the largest number of these cables the conduit may hold?
questions.why: Allowed area = 40% of 390 = 156 mm², and 156 ÷ 14 = 11.1, so 11 cables: always round down. 27 comes from forgetting the 40% and filling the whole bore, which the cables could not be pulled into without damage.

questions.q: To shorten the offset, Dwight thinks about using two 45° bends instead of two 30° bends. What would that change?
o: The offset gets longer, and the route loses 30° of bending
Nothing, since only the 90° bends count towards the limit
The offset gets shorter, but the route gains 30° of bends
The route gains 90° of bending, but the shrink disappears
questions.why: Two 45° bends add 90° instead of 60°, so the total rises by 30°, to 450°. Steeper bends give a shorter offset, but every extra degree of bending makes the cables harder to pull in.

questions.q: What most likely turned the 30° offset into a single 60° change of direction?
o: The two bend marks were 30 mm too close together
The conduit was not turned before the second bend
The take-up for a 90° bend was used by mistake
The conduit was reamed only after it was bent
questions.why: An offset is two equal bends in opposite directions. After the first bend the conduit must be turned exactly half a turn (180°); without the turn, the two 30° bends go the same way and add up to 60°.

questions.q: What should be fitted on the inside of the knockout entry to the adaptable box?
o: A male bush, screwed tight into the coupling
Nothing more, as the coupling holds the conduit
A rubber grommet, to protect the cable sheaths
Insulating tape wrapped round the conduit end
questions.why: A male bush (or a locknut and bushing) clamps the box wall against the coupling, making a tight joint for the earth path, and its smooth mouth protects the cables. Without it the joint can work loose and the cut edge can damage the insulation.

questions.q: What should be done about the sagging bends on the run with saddles at an even 1.5 m?
o: Leave them, as even 1.5 m spacing gives the neatest run
Tighten the existing saddles harder so the bends lift
Pack the gap behind the bends with timber wedges
Add a saddle close to each side of each bend
questions.why: Spacing tables give the largest gap between supports, but a run also needs a saddle close to each box and each side of every bend, often within about 300 mm. Even spacing that misses the bends lets them sag and strains the joints.

questions.q: The ohmmeter reads 0.3 Ω with its leads touching. What should Tamara do before she tests the runs?
o: Change to the insulation resistance range and try again
Add 0.3 Ω to every reading to allow for the joints
Null the leads, or take 0.3 Ω off every reading
Use the meter as it is, since 0.3 Ω is very small
questions.why: The leads have resistance of their own. Nulling them, or subtracting their resistance, means each reading shows only the conduit path. On runs that should read about 0.1 Ω, an extra 0.3 Ω would hide the difference between a good joint and a bad one.

questions.q: Which conduit finish is the best choice for the laundry?
o: Hot-dip galvanised conduit, boxes and fittings
Black enamelled conduit, painted again once fixed
Galvanised conduit with black enamelled boxes
Black enamelled conduit, as the laundry is indoors
questions.why: Constant humidity soon rusts black enamel wherever it is scratched, cut or threaded. Hot-dip galvanising protects the steel, and using the same finish throughout avoids corrosion where different finishes meet at the joints.

questions.q: The builder's hole into the linen store is much bigger than the sealant allows. What should Odane do?
o: Fill the whole 40 mm gap with extra sealant on each face
Make the hole good to the tested size, then seal it
Pack the gap with paper, then cover it with the sealant
Fill the gap with draught-proofing foam and paint it red
questions.why: A fire-stopping product only works as it was tested: here, for gaps up to 15 mm. A larger gap must first be made good, for example with mortar or a product approved for that size, then sealed as the detail says. Photograph and record it before it is hidden.

questions.q: Why should the steam pipe 50 mm from the conduit concern Odane?
o: The pipe will make the steel conduit expand and kink
The pipe will pick up voltage from the conduit run
The heat will make the conduit's earth path weaker
The heat lowers the current the cables can carry
questions.why: Cables are rated for a given surrounding temperature. A hot pipe close by heats the conduit, so the cables can safely carry less current and their insulation ages faster. Keep the separation the specification asks for, or move the run.

questions.q: A steel conduit runs from a cold, air-conditioned server room into a hot, humid corridor. Water is found in its corridor box every morning. What is the best cure?
o: Drill small holes along the top of the run to let air in
Fill every box on the run with grease to keep water out
Seal the conduit where it passes between the two areas
Change to a larger conduit so that air moves through it
questions.why: Warm, damp air moving through the conduit cools in the cold section and leaves its water behind. Sealing the conduit at the boundary with a suitable compound stops the air moving; the NEC asks for this where a raceway passes between areas of very different temperature.

questions.q: A specification says every steel conduit must carry a separate green grounding (earth) conductor, even though the conduit is bonded. Why might the designer ask for this?
o: Because steel conduit cannot carry any fault current at all
So earthing does not rely on each joint staying tight
So the conduit no longer needs bonding at the board
Because a green conductor lowers the conduit fill
questions.why: Steel conduit can be an earth path, but a joint that rusts or works loose breaks it. A separate protective conductor keeps the earth path complete even if one joint fails; the conduit is still bonded as well.
